{"id": "55:9/q09", "question": "How are the commands in this verse linked grammatically to the preceding balance clause?", "turns_on": "Whether the prior clause is an explanatory prohibition, a rationale coordinated with the command, or a purpose clause.", "positions": [{"id": "55:9/q09/p1", "position": "The command explains or follows the preceding ban on transgression.", "reasons": "Zajjaj says fair weight and no short measure confirm taking the earlier words as a prohibition. Razi says establishing weight justly explains not exceeding the balance at 55:8. Alusi coordinates the imperative with the negated clause by reading it as a verbal noun; another parsing makes the earlier lā prohibitive for parallelism. Ibn Ashur coordinates with the earlier prohibition if it is explanatory. Tabatabai reads an as explanatory, lā taṭghaw as prohibition, aqimu as a coordinated command and lā tukhsiru as a second prohibition reinforcing the first. Study Quran distinguishes the warning against tyranny or oppression from the command against withholding another's due, citing 11:84 and 83:1-3."}, {"id": "55:9/q09/p2", "position": "The command coordinates with 'He set the balance' and states its rationale.", "reasons": "Ibn Ashur gives this coordination when the prior clause supplies a rationale; Tabatabai says fair weighing follows naturally from the institution of the balance."}, {"id": "55:9/q09/p3", "position": "The earlier an is a subjunctive purpose clause, 'lest you transgress'.", "reasons": "Tabatabai rejects this parsing because it makes coordination of imperatives with a statement strained; Study Quran reports a subjunctive warning against tyranny and oppression."}]}
{"id": "55:9/q10", "question": "How does fair weighing relate to the balance established in the preceding verses?", "turns_on": "Whether the earlier balance is chiefly a physical scale or a general standard whose practical instance is fair weighing.", "positions": [{"id": "55:9/q10/p1", "position": "The verse applies the ordinary scale instituted by God to fair transactions.", "reasons": "Tabatabai most likely takes the preceding balance as an ordinary scale and this command as its explanation, barring excess and short measure. Kashshaf says God placed measuring instruments on earth for judgments and transactions. Muqatil's surrounding exposition places the balance that establishes justice alongside the raised sky and prostrating plants; he says plants prostrate by shifting shadows, the sky stands 500 years above earth, and the following earth supports creatures and palms, wheat and barley; 41:47 is cited for fruits emerging from coverings."}, {"id": "55:9/q10/p2", "position": "Concrete weighing is one application of a universal standard of truth or justice.", "reasons": "Tabatabai presents this consequence if the earlier balance has the broader sense. Ibn Ashur says mizan and surrounding verbs, prepositions and qist support both senses together. Islahi says the signs show God's care for justice, and honest trade applies the cosmic principle in daily life; Kuran Yolu says qist and scales show universal balance enacted in lived situations. Study Quran says the balance is repeated three times to connect divine creation and human transactions."}]}
{"id": "55:9/q11", "question": "What reported incidents or sayings illustrate this verse?", "turns_on": "The notes cite different reports, ranging from practical scale correction to warnings about dishonest weights and a saying on cosmic justice.", "positions": [{"id": "55:9/q11/p1", "position": "Ibn Abbas told a man giving extra to set the scale's pointer upright.", "reasons": "Ibn Abi Hatim reports Ibn Abbas citing God's command to establish weight with justice."}, {"id": "55:9/q11/p2", "position": "Ali tipped a saffron seller's overfull scale and told him to weigh evenly before giving extra.", "reasons": "Wahidi reports the event to support his preferred order: make the beam level first, then give voluntarily."}, {"id": "55:9/q11/p3", "position": "Ibn Abbas warned the Mawali that even small shortfalls ruined earlier peoples.", "reasons": "Tabari reports his appeal to fear God in measuring and weighing and his reminder that God may add without loss to honest measure."}, {"id": "55:9/q11/p4", "position": "A dying neighbor who used different giving and receiving measures suffered a fiery ordeal.", "reasons": "Malik ibn Dinar said the man saw two mountains of fire; his family disclosed the double measures, and destroying them did not relieve him (Bursevi)."}, {"id": "55:9/q11/p5", "position": "The Prophet is reported to say the heavens and earth are founded on justice.", "reasons": "Study Quran gives this report without grading it."}]}
{"id": "55:9/q12", "question": "What moral and social lesson does the verse teach?", "turns_on": "How broadly the command is applied: reciprocal trade, social order, universal justice, or duties toward God.", "positions": [{"id": "55:9/q12/p1", "position": "Give others the fairness one wants, because just measures sustain society.", "reasons": "Qatada makes reciprocity explicit (Thalabi, Qurtubi); Qushayri applies it to receiving food and drink. Islahi says cheating attacks the foundation of the created order and disorder spreads through a society or nation. Kuran Yolu says concrete fairness needs care, good-faith judgment and full effort. Muqatil says the balance establishes justice and forbids fraud; Kashshaf says God's instruments serve fair giving and taking. Ibn Ashur says the sura embeds a call to justice and to giving rights-holders their full due."}, {"id": "55:9/q12/p2", "position": "The repeated positive and negative commands stress the danger of disobeying justice.", "reasons": "Islahi says the Qur'an uses both formulations when disobedience has dangerous consequences. Kuran Yolu sees the use of qist with scale language as a demand to put universal justice into practice. Study Quran treats justice as fundamental to creation and transactions."}, {"id": "55:9/q12/p3", "position": "For duties to God, justice means following revelation without adding to religion.", "reasons": "Kuran Yolu applies the balance principle to worship and religious obligation."}]}
{"id": "55:9/q13", "question": "How does this command clarify the preceding ban on transgressing the balance?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "55:9/q13/p1", "position": "Transgression includes cheating the person for whom one weighs, by wronging, reducing, or exceeding the proper limit.", "reasons": "Ata from Ibn Abbas explains the ban as not cheating the recipient of the weight. Abu Ubayda and Zajjaj gloss transgression as wronging, reducing, or exceeding the limit (Wahidi)."}]}
{"id": "55:9/q14", "question": "How does the command to weigh justly prepare the later refrain addressing humans and jinn?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "55:9/q14/p1", "position": "It establishes the accountable addressees and the moral context before the refrain.", "reasons": "Samarrai says the sura has already taught humans and jinn the Qur'an and commanded them to weigh justly before addressing them in the refrain, so that address follows established context."}]}
{"id": "55:9/q15", "question": "Who is addressed by the plural commands to weigh justly?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "55:9/q15/p1", "position": "Every individual among humanity and jinn, addressed together as two groups.", "reasons": "Samarrai says the dual address embraces humanity and jinn collectively while the plural command applies to each individual in both groups; he compares the two parties or disputants at 22:19 and 49:9."}]}
{"id": "6:151/q01", "question": "How does the invitation answer the surrounding dispute?", "turns_on": "Whether the address is tied to the polytheists' invented bans or explicitly extends to everyone.", "positions": [{"id": "6:151/q01/p1", "position": "It replaces the polytheists' invented food and livestock prohibitions with God's certain revealed duties.", "reasons": "Muqatil excludes their camel taboos; Thalabi, Baghawi, Qurtubi and Ibn Kathir contrast revelation with conjecture; Biqai and Islahi identify God's exclusive authority and the Quraysh's claim to Abraham's religion."}, {"id": "6:151/q01/p2", "position": "The verse announces a universal Islamic law to all hearers.", "reasons": "Ibn Atiyya and Abu Hayyan explicitly include all humanity; Qurtubi says scholars must also explain the lawful and unlawful, citing 3:187."}, {"id": "6:151/q01/p3", "position": "The invitation calls people upward from ignorance and imitation to knowledge and virtue.", "reasons": "Biqai transmits Zamakhshari's ethical reading; Qashani locates the vice in whim ruling what is lawful."}]}
{"id": "6:151/q02", "question": "Whom does the command to come address?", "turns_on": "The immediate audience in context versus the scope of the message.", "positions": [{"id": "6:151/q02/p1", "position": "The Messenger addresses the polytheists in the immediate context.", "reasons": "Abu Hayyan cites the preceding fabricated bans; Ibn Kathir specifies idol worship, banning God's provision, and child-killing."}, {"id": "6:151/q02/p2", "position": "It summons all people to hear the law.", "reasons": "Ibn Atiyya and Abu Hayyan say Muhammad's message is universal; Abu Hayyan adds the same ruling applies even on the narrower immediate address."}]}
{"id": "6:151/q03", "question": "What does تَعَالَوْا۟ mean and suggest?", "turns_on": "Whether the original spatial force remains rhetorically active.", "positions": [{"id": "6:151/q03/p1", "position": "It originally meant come upward from a lower place, then became a general invitation to approach.", "reasons": "Jishumi, Kashshaf, Ibn Atiyya, Qurtubi, Baydawi, Bursevi, Alusi and others derive it from elevation; Qurtubi notes singular and plural forms and 33:28; Tabatabai reports the derivation."}, {"id": "6:151/q03/p2", "position": "Its upward imagery also invites listeners out of ignorance.", "reasons": "Biqai cites Zamak

{"id": "6:151/q04", "question": "What does أَتْلُ mean?", "turns_on": "Whether the terms distinguish first from repeated speech or act from content.", "positions": [{"id": "6:151/q04/p1", "position": "It means recite or read in ordered sequence.", "reasons": "Jishumi allows reading or retelling; Ibn Atiyya, Abu Hayyan and Biqai stress the following of letters or utterances; Tabatabai equates tilawa and qira'a."}, {"id": "6:151/q04/p2", "position": "Tilāwa and qirāʾa are the spoken act; matluw and maqruʾ are what is uttered or the original speech.", "reasons": "Mawardi prefers this distinction; Jishumi and Tabarsi compare a recitation with a retold narration."}, {"id": "6:151/q04/p3", "position": "Tilāwa and qirāʾa are first utterances, while matluw and maqruʾ are repetitions.", "reasons": "Ali ibn Isa's proposed distinction is reported by Mawardi."}]}
{"id": "6:151/q05", "question": "How does أَتْلُ relate grammatically to the invitation?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "6:151/q05/p1", "position": "The jussive verb answers the imperative invitation: if they come, he will recite.", "reasons": "Alusi states the conditional relation; Jishumi explains the deletion of the initial alif under jussive formation; Bursevi calls it the answer to come."}]}
{"id": "6:151/q06", "question": "What is the grammatical function of مَا حَرَّمَ رَبُّكُمْ?", "turns_on": "Whether recitation governs mā directly, a following question, or a verbal noun.", "positions": [{"id": "6:151/q06/p1", "position": "Mā is chiefly a relative pronoun and object of atlu: recite what the Lord forbade.", "reasons": "Ibn Atiyya prefers this and calls Zajjaj's other construction strained; Samin prefers it, with an omitted resumptive pronoun; Baydawi also permits a relative reading."}, {"id": "6:151/q06/p2", "position": "Mā is governed by ḥarrama, with recitation conveying a question about what the Lord forbade.", "reasons": "Zajjaj links this to 6:145; Ibn Atiyya objects that suspending atlu is strained, and Abu Hayyan and Samin say only verbs of thought permit suspension; Alusi defends it because recitation is a kind of saying."}, {"id": "6:151/q06/p3", "position": "Mā is a verbal noun, 'the prohibition,' standing for the prohibited thing.", "reasons": "Samin explains that a prohibition itself cannot literally be recited; Baydawi allows the verbal noun sense."}, {"id": "6:151/q06/p4", "position": "Mā introduces or is interpreted as an explanatory quotation of the prohibited matter.", "reasons": "Tabarsi records the explanatory possibility alongside the relative and object analyses."}]}
{"id": "6:151/q07", "question": "What does حَرَّمَ mean?", "turns_on": "The narrow lexical ban versus an inclusive sense of firm prescription.", "positions": [{"id": "6:151/q07/p1", "position": "It fundamentally means to prevent or forbid, opposed to releasing or permitting.", "reasons": "Jishumi relates it to ḥajr and ḥaẓr; Tabatabai notes that forbidding can also carry the sense of commanding avoidance."}, {"id": "6:151/q07/p2", "position": "It may denote a fixed and delineated divine prescription in this list.", "reasons": "Razi uses this wider sense to explain why positive duties occur under the introductory wording."}]}
{"id": "6:151/q08", "question": "Where does عَلَيْكُمْ attach?", "turns_on": "Which of the two verbs governs the prepositional phrase.", "positions": [{"id": "6:151/q08/p1", "position": "It attaches to the nearer ḥarrama, stressing what God has prohibited for the hearers.", "reasons": "Qurtubi identifies a Basran analysis; Abu Hayyan says most adopt it; Alusi prefers it for the appeal to the audience's Lordship and need to abstain; Samin notes competing governance."}, {"id": "6:151/q08/p2", "position": "It attaches to atlu, a Kufan competing-governance analysis.", "reasons": "Qurtubi reports the Kufan view; Abu Hayyan attributes preference to Ibn al-Shajari, though his account of proximity differs from Qurtubi's."}]}
{"id": "6:151/q09", "question": "How is أَلَّا تُشْرِكُوا۟ constructed, and how do positive commands enter the list?", "turns_on": "The scope of ḥarrama, whether lā negates or prohibits, and whether a suppressed verb or clause supplies the positive duties.", "positions": [{"id": "6:151/q09/p1", "position": "An is explanatory and lā prohibitive, introducing a jussive prohibition; positive commands also imply bans on their opposites.", "reasons": "Farra favors jussive by the following prohibitions; Zamakhshari invokes implied bans on parental abuse, short measure, unjust speech and broken covenant; Samin defends him; Razi and E lmalili make the entailment explicit. Razi raises the apparent problem that duties appear under what God forbade. Razi objects that on an explanatory parse the coordinated parental kindness can appear forbidden. Burhan reports the prohibitive-lā analysis among the competing parses."}, {"id": "6:151/q09/p2", "position": "A pause after 'your Lord forbade' leaves 'upon you not to associate' as an independent exhortation or obligation.", "reasons": "Ibn al-Anbari and Tabarsi compare 5:105; Itqan defends direct address; Samin and Abu Hayyan call the break weak or distant; Tabatabai rejects imperative-noun ʿalaykum on contextual grounds. Burhan also reports a stop at ḥarrama rabbukum before the following exhortation."}, {"id": "6:151/q09/p3", "position": "An is nominalizing with ordinary negative lā, in nominative or accusative apposition: the recited item is that they not associate.", "reasons": "Nahhas lists accusative apposition and nominative predicate; Ibn Atiyya admits both; Samin prefers the omitted subject 'the recited thing is that you not associate' over 'the forbidden thing'; Alusi sees semantic difficulty. Burhan records ordinary negative lā as another analysis."}, {"id": "6:151/q09/p4", "position": "Anlā is governed by an understood 'I recite the prohibition of shirk' or 'I enjoin you'.", "reasons": "Zajjaj, Wahidi and Baghawi allow both ellipses; the closing waṣṣākum supports the enjoin reading; Abu Hayyan objects that added ellipsis departs from the apparent wording."}, {"id": "6:151/q09/p5", "position": "An is nominalizing; lā is extra, so the forbidden item is association itself.", "reasons": "Baghawi cites 7:12; Thalabi, Samin and Itqan report this; Zamakhshari and Abu Hayyan object that the ensuing positive commands and ordinary prohibitive lā resist it. Burhan records the analysis taking lā as extra."}, {"id": "6:151/q09/p6", "position": "An explains both prohibitions and commands through an omitted 'what He commanded'.", "reasons": "Abu Hayyan proposes the understood phrase; Ibn Kathir cites the closing testament and poetry; Imru al-Qays supplies an example of joining command and prohibition. Jishumi notes that the passage may detail recited commands rather than only forbidden acts."}, {"id": "6:151/q09/p7", "position": "Anlā is governed by an omitted purpose lām: the recital prevents their association.", "reasons": "Zajjaj and Wahidi tie inventing bans to treating others as equal to God; Samin reports objections that this cannot account for following commands; Alusi rejects the strained construction."}, {"id": "6:151/q09/p8", "position": "The verb tushrikū may be subjunctive after an or jussive under prohibitive lā.", "reasons": "Tabarsi and Wahidi note that later clauses can shift mood; Ibn Atiyya prefers the jussive because the prohibited act must remain in the recitation; Tabari adduces rajaz; Samin totals ten syntactic analyses: one genitive, three nominative, six accusative."}, {"id": "6:151/q09/p9", "position": "An is explanatory, but the positive commands coordinate with the opening invitation and recitation.", "reasons": "Abu Hayyan calls this clear, avoiding inclusion of duties under the prohibited acts; Samin reports the same response."}, {"id": "6:151/q09/p10", "position": "Taḥrīm can mean a fixed, clearly delineated divine prescription, embracing both bans and duties.", "reasons": "Razi gives this as a separate answer to the objection that the list contains filial kindness."}]}
{"id": "6:151/q10", "question": "What principle guides choosing among the grammatical analyses?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "6:151/q10/p1", "position": "Prefer the likely, strong and eloquent construction over strained or anomalous parses.", "reasons": "Itqan advises listing plausible alternatives only where no reading clearly prevails; its separate example defends direct-address exhortation here as eloquent."}]}
{"id": "6:151/q11", "question": "What does شَيْـًۭٔا add?", "turns_on": "Whether the indefinite names an object or an act of association.", "positions": [{"id": "6:151/q11/p1", "position": "It can be a cognate or verbal noun, excluding any act or form of association.", "reasons": "Baydawi and Samin allow object versus cognate noun; Alusi includes any form of association."}, {"id": "6:151/q11/p2", "position": "It is an unrestricted object, excluding every possible thing worshipped alongside God.", "reasons": "Ibn Atiyya makes it comprehensive; Alusi includes any thing whatsoever."}]}
{"id": "6:151/q12", "question": "What forms of association does the prohibition cover?", "turns_on": "Whether shirk denotes worship and belief alone or includes obedience and inward attachment.", "positions": [{"id": "6:151/q12/p1", "position": "It forbids worshipping or assigning any partner to God, including idols, celestial bodies, jinn, and attributed children.", "reasons": "Razi relates the four groups to Abraham's argument in 6:74, 6:76; Abu Hayyan and Study Quran enumerate the same partners; Qashani reads serving whim and Satan as idolatry."}, {"id": "6:151/q12/p2", "position": "It also forbids obeying another person in disobedience to God.", "reasons": "Ibn al-Jawzi gives this as a second sense; Elmalili and Qashani connect illicit religious decrees with unauthorized authority."}, {"id": "6:151/q12/p3", "position": "Inwa

{"id": "6:151/q13", "question": "Why is the ban on association placed first?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "6:151/q13/p1", "position": "It is the gravest prohibition and foundation of sound belief and reform.", "reasons": "Biqai says removing vice precedes virtue; Ibn Ashur says belief opens success; Tabatabai calls shirk the greatest injustice, citing 4:116; Elmalili counts nine prohibitions with tawhid as foundation; Kuranyolu calls unity Islam's first condition."}, {"id": "6:151/q13/p2", "position": "It directly counters the preceding polytheist errors and invented prohibitions.", "reasons": "Razi's four groups comprise idol, star, jinn and child-attribution worshippers; Qashani says whims had ruled lawful and forbidden."}]}
{"id": "6:151/q14", "question": "What consequences or assurances are attached to avoiding shirk?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "6:151/q14/p1", "position": "The duty holds even under severe torture.", "reasons": "Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Kathir report Ubadah's seven counsels and warnings even if burned, cut or crucified."}, {"id": "6:151/q14/p2", "position": "Dying without shirk leaves a person eligible for Paradise and forgiveness of lesser sins.", "reasons": "Ibn Kathir cites Abu Dharr's Gabriel report, a sacred report promising forgiveness with hope, 4:48 and 4:116, and Ibn Masud; the reports explicitly mention adultery, theft and wine."}]}
{"id": "6:151/q15", "question": "What does kindness to parents require?", "turns_on": "The minimum legal prohibition and the full positive extent of iḥsān.", "positions": [{"id": "6:151/q15/p1", "position": "It requires positive care, honor, obedience within God's bounds, gentle speech and fulfillment of their rights.", "reasons": "Mawardi and Ibn Abi Hatim list rights and truthful speech; Qurtubi adds freeing them from bondage and avoiding domination; Alusi reports Ibn Abbas's ban on harsh replies, looks and raised voice; Ibn Kathir cites 17:23, 31:15, 2:83, and deeds loved by God; Elmalili forbids obeying parents in shirk."}, {"id": "6:151/q15/p2", "position": "Merely refraining from mistreatment is insufficient; the command also prohibits harming or neglecting parents.", "reasons": "Baydawi and Bursevi emphasize the positive wording; Razi, Nasafi, Biqai, Ibn Ashur, Elmalili and Islahi derive a ban on neglect or scolding. Ibn Kathir notes a variant 'wa-waṣṣā rabbuka' reinforcing the imperative. Samarrai stresses that the positive duty exceeds mere avoidance of harm and reports Bayḍāwī's view that the command forcefully substitutes for a ban on mistreatment because refraining alone is insufficient."}, {"id": "6:151/q15/p3", "position": "Filial service is spiritually transformative.", "reasons": "Bursevi reports a holy man's service to his mother leading to meeting al-Khidr and cites the Persian depiction of Paradise beneath mothers' feet."}]}
{"id": "6:151/q16", "question": "Why does parental kindness immediately follow God's oneness?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "6:151/q16/p1", "position": "Parents are the proximate cause of existence and care, after God as true cause; gratitude and social order require honoring them.", "reasons": "Jishumi, Tabarsi, Razi, Qashani, Biqai, Bursevi, Alusi and Study Quran cite nurture and parental blessing; Tabatabai says family mercy supports procreation, kinship and society; Ibn Kathir and Study Quran cite repeated pairings with worship. Abu Hayyan points readers to the related explanation in 2:83."}, {"id": "6:151/q16/p2", "position": "Disobedience to parents is the greatest sin after shirk.", "reasons": "Qashani links ignorance of parents' rights to ignorance of God's; Bursevi makes the ranking explicit; Tabatabai calls it perhaps the greatest thereafter."}, {"id": "6:151/q16/p3", "position": "The high standing of kindness to parents before God warrants placing it immediately after the ban on association.", "reasons": "Samarrai gives this reason for the matching order here and in 17:23."}]}
{"id": "6:151/q17", "question": "How does إِحْسَٰنًۭا function grammatically?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "6:151/q17/p1", "position": "It is an accusative verbal noun standing for an omitted command to show kindness.", "reasons": "Nahhas calls it a verbal noun; Wahidi coordinates an understood 'do kindness' with not associating; Ibn Atiyya calls it an absolute object; Qurtubi and Ibn Ashur supply the command. Asad reports commentators' agreement that the command is implied."}]}
{"id": "6:151/q18", "question": "Why is الوالدين used for parents?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "6:151/q18/p1", "position": "Commands about goodness, prayer and care consistently use الوالدين rather than الأبوين.", "reasons": "Samarrai adduces 17:23 and 4:36 alongside this verse."}]}
{"id": "6:151/q19", "question": "What child-killing practice and scope does this prohibition address?", "turns_on": "Whether the immediate Arab practice exhausts the ruling or illustrates its wider scope.", "positions": [{"id": "6:151/q19/p1", "position": "It addresses pre-Islamic infanticide, especially burying daughters from poverty or shame, while wording includes sons and daughters.", "reasons": "Ibn Atiyya emphasizes walad includes both; Qurtubi and Ibn Kathir report boys also killed; Thalabi and others mention daughters buried alive; Islahi notes custom and honor; Tabatabai adds fathers' mistaken ownership claim. Damghani and Ibn al-Jawzi's Nuzha note that qatl can itself denote burying daughters or children alive, tying the wording to that practice."}, {"id": "6:151/q19/p2", "position": "The wording reaches killing an unborn child for economic reasons.", "reasons": "Elmalili expressly extends it to abortion; Asad says it may refer to abortions; Kuranyolu says the ban may include unborn children."}, {"id": "6:151/q19/p3", "position": "The prohibition prevents parents from destroying God's creation, descendants and children entrusted to them.", "reasons": "Bursevi cites 11:6; Elmalili says children have a right to life; Islahi calls parents custodians."}]}
{"id": "6:151/q20", "question": "What does إِمْلَٰقٍ mean?", "turns_on": "Whether the root names a state of want, fear of it, hunger, spending, or ruin.", "positions": [{"id": "6:151/q20/p1", "position": "It means poverty, lack or depletion of property and provisions.", "reasons": "Majaz compares amlaqa with property vanishing; Mawardi gives insolvency and a bankrupt person's flattery; Jishumi and Qurtubi discuss the related root; Shammar allows intransitive impoverishment or transitive destruction; Aws ibn Hajar's verse witnesses wealth consumed by calamities; Ibn Atiyya speculates about black stones. Itqan directly glosses imlāq as poverty."}, {"id": "6:151/q20/p2", "position": "It can mean fear of poverty, the motive for killing.", "reasons": "Zajjaj, Nahhas, Ibn Abbas and later sources understand the causal wording this way; Bint al-Shati cites Ibn Abbas's poem about generosity amid poverty."}, {"id": "6:151/q20/p3", "position": "It means hunger in the language of Lakhm.", "reasons": "Muarrij is cited by Ibn Atiyya, Qurtubi and Samin."}, {"id": "6:151/q20/p4", "position": "It means expenditure, spending away property or wasteful extravagance.", "reasons": "Mundhir ibn Said cites a saying ascribed to Ali; Muhammad ibn Nuaym specifies extravagant spending."}, {"id": "6:151/q20/p5", "position": "It can mean ruin or corruption.", "reasons": "Shammar says amlaqa can destroy possessions; Razi, Wahidi and Samin transmit this extension."}]}
{"id": "6:151/q21", "question": "What does مِنْ إِمْلَٰقٍ identify, and how does 17:31 differ?", "turns_on": "Whether min identifies existing poverty specifically or a broader fear of deprivation.", "positions": [{"id": "6:151/q21/p1", "position": "It gives actual present poverty as the motive; 17:31 names fear of future poverty.", "reasons": "Abu Hayyan contrasts present need here with future fear there; Ibn Kathir, Biqai, Samin, Ibn Ashur and Samarrai agree. Bint al-Shati contrasts min with khashyat, citing Bukhari and Abu Ubayda on the root. Itqan and Samarrai distinguish parents already poor here from families with means who fear later want in 17:31. Samarrai quotes al-Baḥr al-Muḥīṭ for this distinction and adds that immediate food is needed to raise the children."}, {"id": "6:151/q21/p2", "position": "It can include fear that supporting children will make rich or poor parents destitute.", "reasons": "Zajjaj and Wahidi use fear; Elmalili says the ban applies rich or poor, and infers that if actual poverty does not excuse killing, future fear is even less an excuse."}]}
{"id": "6:151/q22", "question": "Why are parents' provision and children's provision ordered this way?", "turns_on": "The order of the objects and the force of the fronted divine subject.", "positions": [{"id": "6:151/q22/p1", "position": "Fronting 'We' makes God the exclusive provider and interrupts the ban to remove its excuse.", "reasons": "Ibn Ashur highlights the subject's placement and a shift from third-person Lord to God's direct voice; Razi, Mawardi, Bursevi, Alusi, Elmalili, Tabatabai and Islahi stress divine provision for both generations."}, {"id": "6:151/q22/p2", "position": "Poor parents are reassured first here; in 17:31, those fearing future poverty hear of children's provision first.", "reasons": "Abu Hayyan, Samin, Ibn Kathir, Burhan, Biqai, Ibn Ashur and Samarrai connect pronoun order with the different motives; Samarrai says children bring their own provision. Itqan and Samarrai relate the reversed order to present versus anticipated poverty. Samarrai reports al-Baḥr al-Muḥīṭ's assurance that God undertakes children's provision, and his Lamasat says each generation has its own provision."}]}
{"id": "6:151/q23", "question": "Does the child-killing ban govern contraception or abort
<<part 2 ends; continues in part 3>>

<<chunk 56, part 3 of 0..5>>
ion?", "turns_on": "Whether preventing conception is equivalent to killing existing offspring, and how the ban applies to the unborn.", "positions": [{"id": "6:151/q23/p1", "position": "Withdrawal is prohibited or disliked as hidden infanticide.", "reasons": "Qurtubi reports an analogy from prevention at origin to killing an existing child; a prophetic description of withdrawal as hidden infanticide is used against it, though others take it as dislike. Hasan and Muhammad ibn al-Muthanna read a permissive report as discouragement."}, {"id": "6:151/q23/p2", "position": "Economically motivated abortion falls under the ban, and many contemporary scholars prohibit abortion at every pregnancy stage.", "reasons": "Elmalili extends the general ruling to abortion, Asad mentions economically motivated abortion, and Kuranyolu reports the contemporary majority."}, {"id": "6:151/q23/p3", "position": "Withdrawal is permitted because conception remains under God's decree; a free wife has a consent right.", "reasons": "Qurtubi prefers permissibility, citing Companions, Successors and jurists; Malik and Shafii require a free wife's consent for pleasure and children, unlike a concubine. Kuranyolu cites permissive hadiths and extends the principle to nonharmful contraception."}, {"id": "6:151/q23/p4", "position": "Government population quotas and birth prevention repeat the pre-Islamic distrust of provision.", "reasons": "Islahi says government should develop livelihoods and encourage moderation and work instead of imposing quotas; family planning assumes humans, not God, sustain offspring."}, {"id": "6:151/q23/p5", "position": "Permitted contraception does not make arbitrary avoidance of children proper.", "reasons": "Kuranyolu says procreation is a chief purpose of marriage and discourages avoidance for beauty or convenience, especially where community growth is needed."}]}
{"id": "6:151/q24", "question": "What are the فَوَٰحِش and their apparent and hidden forms?", "turns_on": "Whether the plural remains general or is narrowed to sexual vice, bodily versus inward acts, or reported examples.", "positions": [{"id": "6:151/q24/p1", "position": "They refer especially to sexual transgressions, public prostitution and private illicit lovers.", "reasons": "Muqatil, Ibn Abbas and others describe Jahiliyya tolerating secret adultery while condemning public brothels; Alusi prefers this from the list's sequence and analogy to lost offspring; Elmalili includes zina, sodomy and preliminaries, while Tabatabai says public and secret sexual acts."}, {"id": "6:151/q24/p2", "position": "All grave sins and shameful conduct are banned, whether displayed or concealed.", "reasons": "Jishumi favors the broad reading; Razi, Ibn Atiyya, Tabarsi, Ibn Ashur, Kuranyolu and Study Quran argue the plural and unqualified wording preclude restriction to zina; Ibn Ashur lists public anger and slander, private adultery and theft; Razi and Study Quran connect private restraint to sincere God-consciousness. Zajjaj explicitly includes shirk, child-killing and inventing religious prohibitions among indecencies. Samarrai says the general wording fits a setting where poverty may drive people toward many kinds of wrongdoing."}, {"id": "6:151/q24/p3", "position": "Public forms are visible bodily acts; hidden forms are inward beliefs, desires, intentions or heart-sins.", "reasons": "Tabarsi prefers this as broadest; Mawardi and Ibn Jawzi report beliefs of the heart, Qashani includes desire and intended vice, and Islahi warns of inner vice nourished through senses and thought; Tustari distinguishes limbs from persistence and inward love of sin."}, {"id": "6:151/q24/p4", "position": "Apparent indecencies are forbidden marriages, while hidden indecency is adultery.", "reasons": "Reports differ in examples: marrying mothers or daughters; fathers' wives or two sisters; Ali ibn al-Husayn has father's wife. Ibn Atiyya rejects exhaustive specification; Tabatabai calls them examples only."}, {"id": "6:151/q24/p5", "position": "Outward indecency is wine; inward indecency is adultery.", "reasons": "Dahhak's gloss is repeated by Mawardi, Jishumi, Baghawi, Ibn Jawzi and Thalabi, whose hidden gloss is truncated."}, {"id": "6:151/q24/p6", "position": "Public indecency is wronging others; hidden indecency includes adultery and theft.", "reasons": "Ikrima is transmitted by Ibn Abi Hatim and Durr."}, {"id": "6:151/q24/p7", "position": "The phrase includes specific wrongs such as asking people for things or causeless divorce after miscarriage or childbirth.", "reasons": "Ibn Abi Hatim transmits a Prophetic report on asking and Yahya ibn Jabir on divorce after miscarriage; Durr reports asking and divorce after bearing a child, preserving the report variants."}, {"id": "6:151/q24/p8", "position": "Outward indecency is ostentation; inward indecency is false spiritual claims or action intended for others besides God.", "reasons": "Sulami reports Harith al-Muhasibi on other-directed intention and another authority on display versus false claims."}, {"id": "6:151/q24/p9", "position": "One referent is naked circumambulation of the House.", "reasons": "Ibn Abi Hatim reports Muhammad ibn Qays's addressees and Zuhri's interpretation of Jahiliyyah nakedness."}, {"id": "6:151/q24/p10", "position": "The Prophet named adultery, theft and wine as punishable indecencies.", "reasons": "Durr gives this report, wider than a zina-only gloss."}]}
{"id": "6:151/q25", "question": "How is مَا ظَهَرَ مِنْهَا وَمَا بَطَنَ attached grammatically?", "turns_on": "The appositional syntax and the semantic division it expresses.", "positions": [{"id": "6:151/q25/p1", "position": "The phrase names public conduct and private conduct, both subject to the ban.", "reasons": "Abd al-Razzaq reports Ma'mar; Qatada and Ibn Abbas use overt and secret conduct; Kashshaf and others compare 6:120."}, {"id": "6:151/q25/p2", "position": "It is an accusative apposition or inclusive substitute for al-fawāḥish.", "reasons": "Zajjaj, Nahhas, Qurtubi, Baydawi, Nasafi and Samin agree; Samin also permits partitive min and says the second minhā is elided."}]}
{"id": "6:151/q26", "question": "Why say 'do not approach' indecencies?", "turns_on": "Whether the warning is framed as avoiding outward means or inward beginnings.", "positions": [{"id": "6:151/q26/p1", "position": "It intensifies the ban to include preliminaries, occasions and means leading to commission.", "reasons": "Biqai says prohibition of proximity is stronger; Alusi warns approach invites commission; Ibn Ashur calls closeness metaphorical because sins lack a literal place; Elmalili extends it to sexual preliminaries; Kuranyolu requires avoiding conditions that lead to sin."}, {"id": "6:151/q26/p2", "position": "It calls for uprooting inward vice before it becomes action.", "reasons": "Islahi says vice starts in the heart, grows through senses and thoughts, and can grip a person even when unacted."}]}
{"id": "6:151/q27", "question": "Why does God forbid open and hidden indecencies?", "turns_on": "The notes supply divine jealousy and moral-social consequences as distinct grounds.", "positions": [{"id": "6:151/q27/p1", "position": "Both forms corrupt the person or society, regardless of whether people see them.", "reasons": "Razi says secret sin after public restraint values people's censure over God's judgment; Tabatabai says permissive sexual wrong erodes stigma, lineage and family life; Study Quran reports the public/private piety contrast."}, {"id": "6:151/q27/p2", "position": "Divine jealousy rejects both public and secret sexual wrongdoing.", "reasons": "Ibn Kathir cites Ibn Masud, Sa'd ibn Ubada and Abu Hurayra reports; he notes Abu Hurayra's route is transmitted only by Ibn Mardawayh, though the chain has a parallel."}]}
{"id": "6:151/q28", "question": "What inward meanings are drawn from the ban on indecencies?", "turns_on": "Different accounts of the heart's vice and proper discipline.", "positions": [{"id": "6:151/q28/p1", "position": "Inward vice can be intention, desire, ostentation or serving another than God.", "reasons": "Sulami gives Harith al-Muhasibi's intention gloss; Qashani includes desire and concealed prohibited acts; Bursevi includes illicit looking and acts that distance one from truth."}, {"id": "6:151/q28/p2", "position": "Outward vice belongs to the limbs; inward vice includes persistence, cravings and ready willingness to sin.", "reasons": "Tustari says loving an unavailable sin is persistence; Sahl counts craving even lawful food and extending one's present state into tomorrow as persistence."}, {"id": "6:151/q28/p3", "position": "The heart's obligatory worship is stillness joined to knowledge and certainty.", "reasons": "Tustari defines this inward duty; he also says prophets can repent from outward acts and therefore can have irrelevant thoughts."}]}
{"id": "6:151/q29", "question": "Who is the protected ٱلنَّفْسَ?", "turns_on": "Whether inviolability is restricted to believers or includes covenant-protected others.", "positions": [{"id": "6:151/q29/p1", "position": "It is any inviolable life, including Muslims and protected non-Muslims under covenant or treaty.", "reasons": "Thalabi, Baghawi, Ibn Atiyya and many later authors make the scope explicit; Qurtubi uses generic al-nafs and 70:19–22, 103:1–3; Alusi excludes hostile combatants and rejects Ibn Jubayr's restriction; Ibn Ashur says the generic singular encompasses persons."}, {"id": "6:151/q29/p2", "position": "It is specifically the life of a believer.", "reasons": "Said ibn Jubayr is reported by Ibn Abi Hatim and Durr; Alusi objects that covenant-protected lives also count."}]}
{"id": "6:151/q30", "question": "What does حَرَّمَ ٱللَّهُ convey about the soul?", "turns_on": "Whether the wording primarily names the prohibited act or sanctifies the person.", "positions": [{"id": "6:151/q30/p1", "position": "Its killing has been forbidden from ancient times; attaching the ban to the person emphas
<<part 3 ends; continues in part 4>>

<<chunk 56, part 4 of 0..5>>
izes sanctity.", "reasons": "Ibn Ashur traces the norm to Adam and explains the metonymy; Kuranyolu also calls life inviolable from Adam onward."}, {"id": "6:151/q30/p2", "position": "It may mean God has made the soul itself inviolable, like a sacred precinct.", "reasons": "Ibn Ashur cites 5:1, 27:91 and a hadith on Medina's sanctuary; Tabatabai likewise offers revealed protection from loss of life or rights."}]}
{"id": "6:151/q31", "question": "What does killing إِلَّا بِٱلْحَقِّ allow?", "turns_on": "The general exception requires legal specification; sources differ on how many additional cases it covers.", "positions": [{"id": "6:151/q31/p1", "position": "Only killing authorized by a valid right: chiefly retaliation, married adultery and apostasy.", "reasons": "Prophetic three-case reports are cited by Thalabi, Mawardi, Baghawi, Razi, Ibn Kathir and others; Wahidi transmits Ibn Abbas's narrower qiṣāṣ gloss; Tabatabai groups rightful cases as retaliation and legal penalty. Uthman protests innocence of the three while besieged; Tirmidhi calls a version ḥasan."}, {"id": "6:151/q31/p2", "position": "The lawful grounds also encompass brigandage, rebellion, defense, war and other specified legal penalties.", "reasons": "Jishumi names rebellion, brigandage and self-defense; Razi cites 5:33; Qurtubi discusses zakat refusal, prayer, competing caliphs, same-sex intercourse, armed rebellion and 49:9; Ibn Ashur distinguishes jihad from this exception, adds prisoners and prescribed penalties; Asad includes defensive war and self-defense; Study Quran cites 5:33."}, {"id": "6:151/q31/p3", "position": "The default is sanctity; any permission requires separate sound evidence and lawful cause.", "reasons": "Razi and Elmalili insist a protected life may not be killed without separate proof; Ibn Ashur requires law and sound reason; Tabatabai invokes prescribed right; Asad warns against brute force for private interests; Qurtubi cites reports that killing a protected non-Muslim bars Paradise, with forty- and seventy-year scent variants. Burhan explains that the negation is conditional: killing is barred outside a rightful cause, rather than absolutely in every circumstance."}, {"id": "6:151/q31/p4", "position": "Some cited reports add withholding zakat or abandoning prayer as grounds.", "reasons": "Qurtubi appeals to Abu Bakr's fight against zakat-refusers and 9:5; Ibn Ashur lists persistent prayer refusal after its time and zakat-refusers in relevant circumstances."}]}
{"id": "6:151/q32", "question": "How does إِلَّا بِٱلْحَقِّ qualify killing grammatically?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "6:151/q32/p1", "position": "It qualifies the killer's circumstance, the cause of killing, or an understood kind of killing.", "reasons": "Samin allows a circumstantial qualifier or an adjective of an omitted killing; Alusi extends it to all circumstances, causes or kinds; Ibn Ashur says the preposition marks circumstance or cause. Burhan treats the exception as limiting the prohibited killing to killing without right. He compares prohibitions qualified by a state, such as dying only as Muslims and praying in humility, where the target is the disallowed condition."}]}
{"id": "6:151/q33", "question": "Why specify unlawful killing after banning indecencies and infanticide?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "6:151/q33/p1", "position": "The specific ban emphasizes murder's gravity and allows an explicit rightful exception.", "reasons": "Jishumi, Tabarsi, Razi, Abu Hayyan and Samin make this rationale; Ibn Kathir notes the repetition; Tabatabai reports it as a proposal, while Biqai says child-killing is prohibited repeatedly."}, {"id": "6:151/q33/p2", "position": "Its violation destroys public security and the structure of society.", "reasons": "Tabatabai gives this consequence; Ibn Ashur says this verse's first set preserves life and ends mutual killing."}]}
{"id": "6:151/q34", "question": "What inward meaning is given to killing and life here?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "6:151/q34/p1", "position": "The deeper death is dying in pursuit of God, while one killed in His path remains alive with Him.", "reasons": "Bursevi joins this reflection to an anecdote in which a dead, handsome youth told Abu Saʿid al-Kharraz that lovers live after death, moving from one home to another."}]}
{"id": "6:151/q35", "question": "What does ذَٰلِكُمْ وَصَّىٰكُم بِهِۦ refer to and mean?", "turns_on": "The referent and nuance of the testament formula, and a proposed lexical distinction.", "positions": [{"id": "6:151/q35/p1", "position": "It points collectively to the preceding five commands and calls them God's firm, compassionate charge.", "reasons": "Nahhas allows 'that is the command' or 'God clarified and commanded'; Ibn Abi Hatim reports Ibn Abbas glossing the testament as God's religion; Ibn Atiyya cites poetry; Razi, Abu Hayyan and Alusi explain the tender presentation; Ibn Ashur says singular demonstrative can refer to a set."}, {"id": "6:151/q35/p2", "position": "The wording affirms a decisive command and renewed covenant.", "reasons": "Qurtubi parses the attached address pronouns as vocative, subject pronoun as God; Samin allows demonstrative as subject with verbal predicate or accusative under an omitted verb; Alusi calls the nominal form emphatic."}, {"id": "6:151/q35/p3", "position": "Waṣṣā and awṣā both mean enjoin, though one later distinction assigns the former to religion and latter to worldly matters.", "reasons": "Jishumi equates them; Samarrai contrasts religious counsel with worldly inheritance and cites 19:31 as an exception."}]}
{"id": "6:151/q36", "question": "Why end with لَعَلَّكُمْ تَعْقِلُونَ?", "turns_on": "The immediate sense of reasoning and why this ending differs from the next two.", "positions": [{"id": "6:151/q36/p1", "position": "Reason lets people understand duties, discern benefit and harm, restrain themselves and comply.", "reasons": "Mawardi gives understanding or rational avoidance of punishment; Jishumi, Tabarsi, Ibn Atiyya, Abu Hayyan, Razi and Alusi stress grasping benefit and self-restraint; Samin calls reason the basis of responsibility; Tabatabai says these five are apparent once passions no longer obscure judgment."}, {"id": "6:151/q36/p2", "position": "The first ending suits obvious prohibitions heedlessly violated; later endings concern remembrance and piety.", "reasons": "Qutb al-Razi connects heedlessness with reason and familiar duties with memory; Imam Razi instead distinguishes obvious first duties and subtler later duties; Alusi stresses restraint in mostly negative first set; Biqai and Islahi see a progression through reason, remembrance, then taqwa. Itqan says shirk, neglect of parents, infanticide despite God's provision, indecency, and killing from rage oppose sound judgment and reason's recognition of divine oneness, explaining this first ending."}, {"id": "6:151/q36/p3", "position": "Laʿalla expresses hope from the human hearer's perspective.", "reasons": "Ibn Atiyya says God wants reason to distinguish benefit from harm, while hope belongs to the audience's viewpoint."}]}
{"id": "6:151/q37", "question": "How do these commandments form the verse group and connect to the sūra?", "turns_on": "How the five duties relate to the next two sections and to the preceding controversy.", "positions": [{"id": "6:151/q37/p1", "position": "The list mixes positive and negative duties, and each form implies the opposite.", "reasons": "Kashshaf, Nasafi, Biqai, Elmalili, Ibn Ashur and Islahi explain why commands appear under an opening about prohibitions; Tabatabai says recitation reproduces revelation's mixed form. Tabarsi says forbidding shirk and commanding its avoidance are equivalent."}, {"id": "6:151/q37/p2", "position": "The three sections set social, economic and religious order, each sealed by God's testament.", "reasons": "Ibn Ashur distinguishes belief and family in the first, orphan property and justice in the second, and the straight path in the third; Biqai says the repeated closure strengthens acceptance; Islahi links Abraham's and Moses' guidance. Kashshaf explains the fatha reading of the straight-path clause in 6:153 with an omitted causal lām and says the kasra reading conveys the same cause, supported by 72:18."}, {"id": "6:151/q37/p3", "position": "They restate Abraham's religion and expose Quraysh's neglect beneath invented food taboos.", "reasons": "Islahi describes 6:145–154 as a reply to idolaters who claimed God ordained their way; 16:90 supplies a parallel criterion of justice and goodness; Kuranyolu identifies nine principal duties plus the straight path."}, {"id": "6:151/q37/p4", "position": "The first verse begins with wrongs apparent to sound reason: shirk, filial neglect, infanticide, indecency and murder.", "reasons": "Tabatabai groups the five, and Ibn Ashur says they establish right belief, stable family and protected life."}]}
{"id": "6:151/q38", "question": "What status do these commandments have across revealed scriptures?", "turns_on": "Whether the label emphasizes universal fixed law or a particular identification with Moses' tablets.", "positions": [{"id": "6:151/q38/p1", "position": "They are decisive, universal and unabrogated commandments, the Mother of the Book.", "reasons": "Ibn Abbas reports them as the muhkamāt of 3:7, common to all scriptures, with Paradise for observance and Hell for neglect; Ibn Atiyya and Qurtubi mention the Ten Commandments identification. Elmalili counts nine listed prohibitions with tawhid as their first foundation. Ibn Kathir reports Ibn Abbas calling them foundations of scripture."}, {"id": "6:151/q38/p2", "position": "They correspond to the ten commandments given to Moses.", "reasons": "Ibn Atiyya, Qurtubi and Abu Hayyan transmit this identification; Itqan and Elmalili give lists including monotheism, false oath, filial duty, murder, adultery, theft, testimony, coveting and Sabbath rules."}]}

t do reports say about the opening of the Torah?", "turns_on": "The wording and count of the reported Torah correspondence.", "positions": [{"id": "6:151/q39/p1", "position": "Kaʿb says this opening command or the ten commandments were first in the Torah.", "reasons": "Thalabi, Ibn Atiyya, Tabarsi, Qurtubi, Abu Hayyan, Durr, Itqan, Elmalili and Alusi transmit variants: first thing, first verse with basmala, or first ten revealed verses."}, {"id": "6:151/q39/p2", "position": "Some describe them more generally as the ten commandments revealed to Moses.", "reasons": "Ibn Atiyya, Qurtubi and Abu Hayyan present this alongside Ibn Abbas's universal-commandment report."}]}
{"id": "6:151/q40", "question": "What is said of the Prophet's sealed testament and the pledge on these verses?", "turns_on": "Distinct reported uses of the verses as testament, pledge, and prophetic address.", "positions": [{"id": "6:151/q40/p1", "position": "Ibn Masud calls 6:151–153 the Prophet's sealed written testament.", "reasons": "Ibn Abi Hatim, Ibn Kathir, Durr, Alusi and Tirmidhi transmit it; Tirmidhi grades it ḥasan gharīb, while Alusi says ḥasan."}, {"id": "6:151/q40/p2", "position": "The Prophet took a pledge on the commands: fulfillment is rewarded; a breach may be punished here or left to God's will after death.", "reasons": "Ibn Abi Hatim gives seven traits and the punishment-or-pardon rule; Ibn Kathir says Hakim graded the extended report authentic while the two Sahihs have shorter pledges; Durr and Alusi repeat the three-verse pledge, with worldly punishment expiating."}, {"id": "6:151/q40/p3", "position": "Al-Rabi ibn Khuthaym treated the verses as a sealed letter or written counsel from the Prophet.", "reasons": "Thalabi, Qurtubi and Durr report reciting them to a companion and writing them for a questioner."}, {"id": "6:151/q40/p4", "position": "At Mina, the Prophet recited the commandments to a tribe while inviting them to monotheism, messenger-belief and protection.", "reasons": "Durr names Mafruq and Hani's approval, a following recital of 16:90, a promise concerning Persian lands, and a quotation of 33:45 before the Prophet left with Abu Bakr."}, {"id": "6:151/q40/p5", "position": "At the Farewell Pilgrimage the Prophet named shirk, unlawful killing, adultery and theft as prohibitions.", "reasons": "Durr transmits this four-item report."}]}
{"id": "6:151/q41", "question": "What is reported about the revelation and virtue of al-Anʿām?", "turns_on": "Whether the sūra came all at once and which verses, if any, were Medinan; reports also differ on escorting angels.", "positions": [{"id": "6:151/q41/p1", "position": "These three verses, 6:151–153, were a Medinan exception.", "reasons": "Ibn Abbas and Shahr ibn Hawshab report this against the whole-sūra Meccan account; Study Quran notes early claims of some Medinan verses. Itqan transmits Abu Amr's report of Mujahid asking Ibn Abbas for a Meccan-Medinan list, in which Ibn Abbas excepts the three verses beginning 'Come'; the author accepts a sound Ibn Abbas report for this three-verse exception."}, {"id": "6:151/q41/p2", "position": "The sūra descended as a whole in Mecca, accompanied by angels.", "reasons": "Reports vary in count: one thousand, seventy thousand, or five hundred, and one describes ranks from heaven to earth; the Prophet saw the horizon filled. Ali's report says usual revelation was five verses at a time and claims its recitation heals the ill."}, {"id": "6:151/q41/p3", "position": "Other reports except 6:91 or 6:111 from the Meccan revelation.", "reasons": "Kalbi locates 6:91 with a Jewish man who denied revelation; Abu Juhayfa excepts 6:111."}, {"id": "6:151/q41/p4", "position": "A weakly transmitted report promises Paradise to one who loves and recites al-Anʿām.", "reasons": "Durr attributes it to Anas and labels its transmission weak."}, {"id": "6:151/q41/p5", "position": "Al-Anʿām is Meccan except six verses, including the final passage beginning 'Say: Come'.", "reasons": "Burhan says reports establish a six-verse exception and identifies this closing passage among them."}, {"id": "6:151/q41/p6", "position": "Al-Anʿām is Meccan except this verse and the following verse.", "reasons": "Itqan reports Bishr's statement transmitted through Sufyan and Layth that the exception begins 'Say: Come' and includes the next verse."}]}
{"id": "6:151/q42", "question": "What do the commands imply about human acts and restraint?", "turns_on": "Human moral agency and whether deliberate restraint counts as an act.", "positions": [{"id": "6:151/q42/p1", "position": "People are unforced, responsible agents whose choices merit reward and punishment.", "reasons": "Jishumi says God leaves people free for testing and evidence-based obedience, against the Compulsionists' view of created human acts; he condemns habit, imitation, doubt, neglect of inquiry and worldly motives."}, {"id": "6:151/q42/p2", "position": "Refraining from a forbidden act is itself an obligatory act with deserved reward or punishment.", "reasons": "Tabarsi identifies this as his school's principle and takes the verse as evidence."}]}
{"id": "6:151/q43", "question": "Why is the divine agent named with the prohibitions here?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "6:151/q43/p1", "position": "The Qur'an names God when explicitly attributing a ruling to Him.", "reasons": "Burhan contrasts explicit attribution here with omitted agents in references to sexual intercourse or forbidden foods and named agents in permission for marriage contracts."}]}
{"id": "6:151/q44", "question": "Why does al-Isrāʾ expand the command about worship beyond this verse?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "6:151/q44/p1", "position": "Its fuller context calls both for rejecting another deity and for worshipping God alone, where al-Anʿām states the ban briefly.", "reasons": "Samarrai compares this verse with 17:22–23 and relates the fuller wording there to that passage's expanded style."}]}
{"id": "6:151/q45", "question": "Why are indecencies prohibited generally here while al-Isrāʾ singles out adultery?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "6:151/q45/p1", "position": "Present poverty can incite many sins, while al-Isrāʾ addresses wealthy people whose costly pursuits include adultery.", "reasons": "Samarrai makes this contextual comparison with 17:32.
